name: OpenSSL 'Heartbleed'
defect: The TLS heartbeat handler copied a claimed payload length without checking it against the record, leaking up to 16 KiB of process memory. The vulnerable releases are OpenSSL 1.0.1a..1.0.1f; the fixed release is 1.0.1g (the CVE-2014-0160 fix release). The probe (src/hb.c) performs the exact historical exploit message sequence — ClientHello with the heartbeat extension, then the malformed heartbeat immediately after ServerHelloDone — against the linked library's own protocol code. On the leak path the probe dumps the echoed heartbeat-response bytes to stdout, so the leaked CONTENT is observable evidence (the memory.leak.sensitive axis).

build.official_tarballs: the 7 OpenSSL 1.0.1 tarballs from openssl.org, pinned by SHA-256 in build/build-manifest.json

leak_study.comparator: comparators/heartbleed-leak.py (relation eq, extractor leak-scan, kind text)
leak_study.normalizer: normalizers/strip-heap-noise.py (masks ASLR-style hex runs on stdout)
leak_study.minimizer: minimizers/heartbeat-length.py (kappa route leak-minimize; reduces the claimed payload length)
leak_study.mutation: mutations/seed-leak.py (operator seed-leak; proposes a mutant that dumps a seeded PEM key + SECRET_KEY)
leak_study.minimal_trigger: claimed payload length 0x0FE9 (4073) — the empirically minimal claim that yields the observable leak on 1.0.1f; below it the response is constructed but never flushed to the wire
leak_study.evidence: evidence/ (regenerated by study.sh / reproduce.sh run; deterministic content-addressed ids)
leak_study.claim: claims/heartbleed-trajectory.md (the comparative claim + the measured lifecycle table)

challenge: seed-leak (the sensitivity proof: a seeded leak must be seen on memory.leak.sensitive and nothing else)

clean_control.expectation: no residual on any axis (with the handshake-only clean fixture, the vulnerable and fixed builds are byte-identical on exit and stderr)
